note: Comparative trust law across the four job campaign states plus Nevada as benchmark. Every row names the statute it rests on, because the point is to be able to say WHICH provision does the work rather than which state has the better reputation. Sourced from Kristian's own primary law library, compiled from official state legislature sites, and it carries the corrections he verified. Where the library does not hold a statute, the row says so rather than guessing.

features.name: putting your own assets in a trust your future creditors cannot reach
features.plain: a self settled asset protection trust, sometimes called a DAPT
features.why_it_comes_up: Someone in a profession that gets sued, or someone about to sell a business, asks whether they can put their own money in a trust and still benefit from it.

DE.cite: 12 Del. C. 3570 to 3576, Qualified Dispositions in Trust Act

TN.cite: Tenn. Code Ann. 35-16-101 through 112, Tennessee Investment Services Act of 2007

NV.cite: NRS 166, Spendthrift Trust Act of Nevada
NV.note: 166.040 permits the settlor as a beneficiary; 166.170 sets the limitations period.

NC.note: North Carolina has no DAPT statute, and this section runs the other way: a creditor reaches the maximum that could be distributed to the settlor, spendthrift language notwithstanding.

features.name: how many generations a trust can run before it has to end
features.plain: a dynasty trust, and the rule against perpetuities that limits one
features.why_it_comes_up: Someone wants the trust to hold for grandchildren and beyond, usually alongside a generation skipping exemption allocation.

DE.note: Perpetual for personal property; 110 years for real property held directly in trust.

SD.note: Abolishes the common law rule against perpetuities outright.

NC.note: Perpetuities and suspension of the power of alienation. The chapter is on file; read it directly rather than relying on a chart.

features.name: splitting the trustee's job so someone else directs the investments
features.plain: a directed trust, with a trust protector or an investment adviser
features.why_it_comes_up: A family wants a corporate trustee for administration but wants to keep their own investment adviser, or wants concentrated stock or a family business held without the trustee forced to diversify it.

SD.note: Excluded fiduciary, trust protector, and the investment, distribution and tax advisers.

NC.note: North Carolina's own 2012 power holder framework. This is NOT the Uniform Directed Trust Act, so do not reason from UDTA commentary.

NV.note: The library does not hold Nevada's directed trust statute.

features.name: pouring an irrevocable trust into a better one without going to court
features.why_it_comes_up: An old irrevocable trust has terms that no longer fit: a beneficiary on public benefits, a bad trustee succession clause, or a distribution standard that will hurt someone.

DE.note: Trustee authority to invade principal. Nonuniform.

TN.cite: Tenn. Code Ann. 35-15-818, Trustee's power to appoint in trust
TN.note: CORRECTION he verified: nearly every chart still cites 35-15-816(b)(27), which now reads deleted by 2021 amendment. The operative authority is 35-15-818, added by 2023 Tenn. Acts ch. 166 s 17, effective April 17, 2023. Section 35-15-1201(a)(14) still carries the dead cross reference, which is how the error keeps spreading.

NC.cite: NCGS 36C Article 8B, North Carolina Uniform Trust Decanting Act, S.L. 2017-121
NC.note: CORRECTION he verified: do not cite 36C-8-816.1, repealed by that same session law effective July 18, 2017. North Carolina can decant, so this is not a gap.

features.name: whether the state taxes income the trust accumulates
features.plain: state fiduciary income tax on a nongrantor trust
features.why_it_comes_up: A trust accumulates income rather than distributing it, and the state where it is administered wants a share.

NC.note: North Carolina is the only one of these five that taxes trust income. Its application narrowed after Kaestner, 588 U.S. 262 (2019), and he flagged the current wording as not yet run to ground. Read the section on file rather than restating the old rule.

DE.cite: 30 Del. C. ch. 16 subch. III, including the 1636 deduction
DE.note: Delaware allows a deduction for income set aside for nonresident beneficiaries. He flagged 30 Del. C. 1601, the resident trust definition, as only partly verified, so do not state the residency rule as settled.

SD.note: No state income tax on trust income.

TN.note: No state income tax on trust income.

NV.note: CORRECTION he verified: the income tax prohibition is section 9, not section 1. A widely circulated link says section 1 and is wrong.

features.name: keeping the trust and its terms out of view
features.plain: quiet trusts, sealing a trust file, and limiting what beneficiaries must be told
features.why_it_comes_up: A family does not want the children to know the size of the trust, or does not want the instrument sitting in a public court file.

NC.note: North Carolina runs the other way on this: the duty to inform qualified beneficiaries is affirmative, and he has written about it.

DE.note: The library does not hold Delaware's quiet trust provision.

SD.note: The library does not hold South Dakota's sealing statute.

open_items: 30 Del. C. 1601, the resident trust definition. Only 1636 was verified.
NCGS 105-160.2 current wording after Kaestner. The amendment history was not run to ground.
Nevada's income tax prohibition is Nev. Const. art. X sec. 9, not sec. 1.
framing: Situs is a live practice question and it is also the fastest way for a non lawyer to give advice by accident. Name the statute that does the work, name what North Carolina does instead, and stop. The choice belongs to a lawyer licensed in the state being considered, working with a tax adviser, because settlor residency, trustee location and where the beneficiaries live all change the answer.
